name: Kente
basis: why: narrow warp-faced bands with weft floats, sewn edge to edge; how: strips of cells, traditional colours, weft-float blocks

lumenary.blurb: Ghanaian strip weaving. Narrow bands are woven on a loom, each one a run of vertical threads broken by blocks of horizontal float, then sewn edge to edge. Colours are snapped to the traditional few.

facts.from: The Asante and Ewe of Ghana
facts.bestOn: Colourful pictures with large areas of colour

why: Kente is woven on a narrow loom that makes a band only about a hand’s breadth wide, and many bands are sewn edge to edge into a cloth. In a warp-faced band the lengthwise threads hide the weft, so the colour you see is the warp, and where the weaver wants a pattern a block of weft is floated across the surface. The result is stripes broken by small blocks, with colours chosen from a traditional few.
how: Make each strip four cells wide, with cells 1.2 times as tall as wide, and offset odd strips by half a cell so blocks do not line up across seams.
Give every cell the nearest of seven cloth colours (gold, red, green, black, blue, white and orange) to the picture’s colour.
Inside a strip, group cells in blocks of three units in height, and float some as horizontal weft.
Show thread relief with light and shade between the threads.
Choose motif blocks with the float slider, and a new weave with the seed.
history: Tradition connects kente with Bonwire, where two hunters are said to have learned to weave by watching a spider. The cloth was long worn by Asante kings and other royalty, and each pattern and colour carries a meaning. Kente is now worn at weddings, graduations and festivals in Ghana and by people across the African diaspora. The word is said to come from kenten, the Asante word for basket.
uses: Fashion, graduation stoles and home textiles
terms: The lengthwise threads on a loom.
The threads that cross the warp.
A thread passed over several others on the surface of the cloth.
paragraphs: Kente is woven by the Asante and the Ewe of Ghana on a narrow loom that makes a band only a hand’s breadth wide. The long bands are cut and sewn edge to edge, and a large cloth uses a couple of dozen of them. In a warp-faced band the lengthwise threads hide the weft completely, so the colour you see is the colour of the warp, and where the weaver wants a pattern a block of weft is floated across on the surface instead. The program follows that structure. Each strip is four cells wide, the cells are as tall as 1.2 of their width, and odd strips are offset by half a cell so that the blocks do not line up across seams.

Every cell takes the nearest of seven cloth colours (gold, red, green, black, blue, white, orange) to your picture’s colour. Inside a strip, blocks of three units in height (a unit is half the strip width) are either warp-faced, drawn as vertical threads with an accent thread on every sixth one, or weft-float blocks that carry a small diamond, zigzag, check or cross motif in the strip’s accent colour. Threads are shaded across their width so each looks like a rounded yarn, and the seam between strips is a dark line at half brightness.

equations.note: Odd strips s are offset by half a cell height h_c; w_s is the strip width.

The chance that a block is a float motif (m is the slider), and the rounded-thread shading: u runs 0 to 1 across one thread and ρ is the thread relief slider. The coefficient is 0.3 for floats and 0.32 for warp threads.

equations.tex: k=\arg\min_j\ d\big(\mathbf c',\mathbf p_j\big),\qquad \mathbf c'=\operatorname{boost}\big(\bar{\mathbf c}\big)
equations.note: The cell colour: the blurred picture colour with saturation raised by 1.5, matched to the cloth palette.

presets.text: Narrow strips give a fine, busy weave.
Wide strips show the blocks of float clearly.
Few float blocks look closer to a plain striped cloth.
